claim: Adult-born neurons are continually produced in the dentate gyrus.
source: Adult-born neurons are continually produced in the dentate gyrus but it is unclear whether synaptic integration of new neurons affects the pre-existing circuit.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of adult neurogenesis, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Enhancing neurogenesis by conditional deletion of the pro-apoptotic gene Bax in stem cells reduced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in mature neurons.
source: Enhancing neurogenesis by conditional deletion of the pro-apoptotic gene Bax in stem cells reduced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and spine density in mature neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the measurements of EPSCs in mature neurons from BaxKOim mice.

claim: Enhancing neurogenesis by conditional deletion of Bax in stem cells reduced spine density in mature neurons.
source: Enhancing neurogenesis by conditional deletion of the pro-apoptotic gene Bax in stem cells reduced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) and spine density in mature neurons
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced spine density in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice.

claim: Genetic ablation of neurogenesis increased EPSCs in mature neurons.
source: whereas genetic ablation of neurogenesis increased EPSCs in mature neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the Ablatedim mouse model showing increased EPSC amplitudes in mature neurons.

claim: Bax deletion in developing and mature dentate neurons increased EPSCs.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that Bax deletion in developing and mature dentate neurons increased EPSCs and prevented neurogenesis-induced synaptic suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from recordings in BaxKO neurons showing enhanced EPSCs.

claim: Bax deletion in developing and mature dentate neurons prevented neurogenesis-induced synaptic suppression.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that Bax deletion in developing and mature dentate neurons increased EPSCs and prevented neurogenesis-induced synaptic suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that neurogenesis-induced loss of synaptic strength to mature GCs was absent in BaxKOmat mice.

claim: Neurogenesis modifies synaptic transmission to mature neurons in a manner consistent with a redistribution of pre-existing synapses to newly integrating neurons.
source: Together these results show that neurogenesis modifies synaptic transmission to mature neurons in a manner consistent with a redistribution of pre-existing synapses to newly integrating neurons
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing inverse relationship between new neuron number and mature neuron EPSCs, with no change in total synapses.

claim: A non-apoptotic function of the Bax signaling pathway contributes to ongoing synaptic refinement within the dentate circuit.
source: and that a non-apoptotic function of the Bax signaling pathway contributes to ongoing synaptic refinement within the dentate circuit.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data showing that Bax deletion affects synaptic transmission independent of its role in cell death, combined with knowledge of Bax's role in synaptic plasticity.

claim: New granule cells integrate into the hippocampal circuit by establishing synapses with existing neurons.
source: Continual neurogenesis in the adult dentate gyrus (DG) produces new granule cells (GCs) that integrate into the hippocampal circuit by establishing synapses with existing neurons (Espósito et al., 2005; Ge et al., 2006; Toni et al., 2008; Dieni et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: New GCs exhibit intrinsic and synaptic properties distinct from mature GCs during a transient period of maturation.
source: During a transient period of maturation, new GCs exhibit intrinsic and synaptic properties distinct from mature GCs, potentially underlying the contribution of neurogenesis to memory encoding (Schmidt-Hieber et al., 2004; Ge et al., 2007; Aimone et al., 2011; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013; Brunner et al., 2014; Dieni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior published work.

claim: Computational models suggest that remodeling of pre-existing circuits by continual neurogenesis can degrade established memories.
source: Yet computational models also suggest that remodeling of pre-existing circuits by continual neurogenesis can degrade established memories (Weisz and Argibay, 2012; Chambers et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: Neurogenesis facilitates 'forgetting'.
source: a possibility that has recently gained experimental support from the observation that neurogenesis facilitates 'forgetting' (Akers et al., 2014; Epp et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Immature dendritic spines transiently receive a high proportion of synapses from multiple-synapse boutons.
source: This possibility is supported by anatomical evidence that immature dendritic spines transiently receive a high proportion of synapses from multiple-synapse boutons (Toni et al., 2007; Toni and Sultan, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Dramatically increasing the number of new neurons does not alter the density of spines and synapses in the molecular layer.
source: Furthermore, dramatically increasing the number of new neurons does not alter the density of spines and synapses in the molecular layer, suggesting a readjustment of synaptic connections (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Adult-born neurons undergo a period of massive cell death during the first weeks after cell birth.
source: Adult-born neurons undergo a period of massive cell death during the first weeks after cell birth that is rescued by deletion of the pro-apoptotic protein Bax (Sun et al., 2004; Kim et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Conditional Bax deletion in Nestin-expressing progenitors enhances the number of adult-born neurons without affecting other cell populations.
source: and conditional Bax deletion in Nestin- expressing progenitors enhances the number of adult-born neurons without affecting other cell populations (Sahay et al., 2011; Ikrar et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Inducible expression of the diphtheria toxin receptor in Nestin-expressing stem cells allows selective ablation of adult-born neurons.
source: Similarly, inducible expression of the diphtheria toxin receptor in Nestin-expressing stem cells allows selective ablation of adult-born neurons (Arruda-Carvalho et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Physiological stimuli like exercise and environmental enrichment enhance dentate neurogenesis.
source: Physiological stimuli like exercise and environmental enrichment also enhance dentate neurogenesis
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of adult neurogenesis.

claim: Neurogenesis was enhanced by 41% in BaxKOim mice compared to controls.
source: Stereological cell counts of eGFP+ newborn cells revealed neurogenesis was enhanced by 41% (control 16,881 ± 1422 cells, n = 4; BaxKOim 23,756 ± 2166 cells, n = 4; unpaired t-test p=0.038).
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological cell count data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: There was no difference in fEPSPs in slices from BaxKOim and control mice.
source: There was no difference in fEPSPs in slices from BaxKOim and control mice (two-way ANOVA, 0.076).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The overall EPSC/FV ratio was reduced in BaxKOim slices compared to controls.
source: Right, the overall EPSC/FV ratio was reduced in BaxKOim slices (unpaired t-test, n = 86, 95).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: There was no difference in the paired-pulse ratio of evoked EPSCs between BaxKOim and control mature GCs.
source: The paired-pulse ratio of evoked EPSCs (100 ms ISI) was similar in BaxKOim and control mature GCs (unpaired t-test p=0.90; n = 15 controls,14 BaxKOim).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Spontaneous EPSCs in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice had lower frequency than controls.
source: Spontaneous EPSCs in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice had lower frequency and similar amplitudes as sEPSCs in mature GCs from control mice (unpaired t-test p=0.027 and 0.79, respectively; n = 11 controls, 9 BaxKOim).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a reduction in the frequency of asynchronous EPSCs in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice.
source: Middle, there was no difference in the average amplitude across genotypes but a reduction in the frequency of aEPSCs (1743 events in 8 GCs from controls, 1015 events in 9 GCs from BaxKOim; unpaired t-test p=0.51 and 0.007 respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The density of dendritic spines was lower in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice compared to controls.
source: Middle, the density of dendritic spines was lower in BaxKOim mice (14 ± 0.8 spines/10 μm, 936 total spines counted on 15 dendritic segments in two control mice; 10 ± 0.6 spines/10 μm, 676 total spines on 12 dendritic segments from 3 BaxKOim mice; p=0.0007 unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by spine density analysis data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the percentage of stubby spines in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice.
source: Classifying spines as stubby, thin and mushroom revealed a significant increase in the percentage of stubby spines in mature GCs from BaxKOim mice (p=0.04 unpaired t-test)
evidence: This claim is supported by spine classification data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a 27% reduction in the number of Dcx-expressing immature cells in Ablatedim mice.
source: Ten days after injections, there was a 27% reduction in the number of Dcx-expressing immature cells in the dentate of Ablatedim mice (Figure 4B; 5601 ± 262, n = 2, compared to 7648 ± 332, n = 4, p=0.016)
evidence: This claim is supported by cell count data from Dcx immunostaining.

claim: There was enhanced synaptic transmission to individual mature GCs in Ablatedim mice, shown by larger EPSC amplitudes across FVs.
source: However, there was enhanced synaptic transmission to individual mature GCs, shown by larger EPSC amplitudes across FVs (Figure 4E) and an overall larger EPSC/FV ratio (2.2 ± 0.1 in control compared to 3.7 ± 0.4 in Ablatedim mice; n = 42, 47 respectively, p=0.001 unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Immature GCs in control mice had lower EPSC/FV ratio than mature GCs.
source: Consistent with the low excitatory connectivity of immature GCs (Dieni et al., 2016), in control mice the EPSC/FV ratio of immature GCs (1.24 ± 0.07 n = 80) was lower than the EPSC/FV ratio in mature GCs (2.44 ± 0.16 n = 86, p<0.0001 unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data comparing immature and mature GCs, with citation to prior work.

claim: EPSCs in BaxKO immature GCs were significantly larger than EPSCs in BaxWT immature GCs across FV bins.
source: But unexpectedly, simultaneously recorded fEPSPs and EPSCs revealed that EPSCs in BaxKO immature GCs were significantly larger than EPSCs in BaxWT immature GCs across FV bins, and the overall EPSC/FV ratio was greater (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5C.

claim: EPSCs in BaxKO GCs were larger than EPSCs in BaxWT GCs at 16 weeks after tamoxifen-induced recombination.
source: Consistent with a role of Bax suppressing synaptic depression, EPSCs in BaxKO GCs were larger than EPSCs in BaxWT GCs (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Western blot analysis revealed no difference in Bax protein levels in hippocampal lysates from BaxKOim and control mice.
source: Western blot analysis revealed no difference in Bax protein levels in hippocampal lysates from BaxKOim and control mice, showing that deletion of Bax from a small percentage of GCs does not lead to widespread changes in Bax protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: EPSCs in BaxKO mature GCs were larger than EPSCs in BaxWT mature GCs across a range of stimulus intensities in BaxKOmature mice.
source: EPSCs in BaxKO GCs were larger than EPSCs in BaxWT GCs across a range of stimulus intensities (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the density of spines in BaxKO mature GCs compared to BaxWT GCs.
source: Posthoc analysis revealed a significant increase in the density of spines in BaxKO mature GCs, with no change in head diameter (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by spine density analysis data presented in Figure 6G.

claim: The number of newborn integrating neurons was enhanced by ~48% in BaxKOmat mice.
source: Stereological cell counts revealed neurogenesis was enhanced by ~48% (control 17,910 ± 900 cells, n = 7; BaxKOmat26,508 ± 2728 cells, n = 6; unpaired t-test), similar to enhanced neurogenesis in BaxKOim mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by stereological cell count data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: There was no difference in EPSCs across FVs between control and BaxKOmat mice.
source: Middle, there was no difference in EPSCs across FVs (two-way ANOVA p=0.990, n = 12 control, 19 BaxKOmat GCs) or in the EPSC/FV ratio (unpaired t-test p=0.387, n = 88 control, 129 BaxKOmat)
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Environmental enrichment enhances neurogenesis to a similar or greater extent as observed in BaxKOim mice.
source: We previously found that housing mice with running wheels alone for four weeks increases the number of POMC-eGFP labeled GCs to 146% of age-matched controls (Overstreet et al., 2004), suggesting that EE enhances neurogenesis to a similar or greater extent as observed in BaxKOim mice (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior published data cited in the manuscript.

claim: The fEPSP slope was enhanced in slices from EE mice with no difference in the FV.
source: As previously reported (Green and Greenough, 1986; Foster et al., 1996), the fEPSP slope was enhanced in slices from EE mice with no difference in the FV, suggesting an increase in total synaptic strength with no change axonal excitability (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data with citations to prior studies.

claim: EPSCs in mature GCs were larger in slices from mice housed in EE.
source: Consistent with the enhanced fEPSPs, EPSCs in mature GCs were larger in slices from mice housed in EE (Figure 8D), such that the overall EPSC/FV ratio was 2.6 ± 0.16 in EE compared to 1.6 ± 0.07 in control (n = 88, 58 respectively, p<0.0001 unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 8D.

claim: There was no difference in the PPR of evoked EPSCs between EE and control mice.
source: We found no difference in the PPR of evoked EPSCs, suggesting that release probability is unchanged (Figure 8E), as previously reported (Foster et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 8E, with citation to prior work.

claim: The frequency of sEPSCs was increased with no change in sEPSC amplitude in mature GCs after EE.
source: However, the frequency of sEPSCs was increased with no change in sEPSC amplitude (Figure 8F), similar to the recently reported increase in miniature EPSCs in mature GCs after EE (Kajimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 8F, with citation to a recent study.

claim: Bax activation is necessary and sufficient to activate caspase-3, which acts as a mediator of activity-dependent hippocampal LTD and synaptic pruning.
source: Since Bax activation is necessary and sufficient to activate caspase-3, which acts as a mediator of activity-dependent hippocampal LTD and synaptic pruning (Li et al., 2010; Jiao and Li, 2011; Ertürk et al., 2014; Lo et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on the role of Bax and caspase-3 in synaptic plasticity.

claim: Caspase-3 KO mice exhibit increased GC spine density.
source: Indeed, local induction of caspase-3 activity in dendrites triggers spine elimination whereas caspase-3 KO mice exhibit increased GC spine density (Ertürk et al., 2014; Lo et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Enhancing neurogenesis by blocking output from mature GCs improves performance on the same context discrimination task.
source: First, both enhancing neurogenesis and blocking output from mature GCs improves performance on the same context discrimination task (Sahay et al., 2011; Nakashiba et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Deletion of Bax signaling in postmitotic GCs enhances synaptic transmission, consistent with increased activation of DG neurons observed in caspase-3-/- mice.
source: Finally, our results showing that deletion of Bax signaling in postmitotic GCs enhances synaptic transmission is consistent with increased activation of DG neurons observed in caspase-3-/- mice, which also show behavioral deficits in attending to relevant stimuli (Lo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citation to a prior study.

claim: Manipulating the number of immature GCs was inversely associated with excitatory synaptic strength of mature GCs.
source: In summary, manipulating the number of immature GCs was inversely associated with excitatory synaptic strength of mature GCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data from BaxKOim and Ablatedim experiments.

claim: Changing the number of newly generated neurons did not alter the total number of afferent axons or synapses.
source: These manipulations did not affect global measures of axonal activation, synaptic strength or presynaptic terminals, suggesting that changing the number of newly generated neurons did not alter the total number of afferent axons or synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing no changes in FVs, fEPSPs, or vGlut1 expression.

claim: Global measures of basal synaptic transmission and release probability are independent of the number of dentate GCs.
source: The idea that global measures of basal synaptic transmission and release probability are independent of the number of dentate GCs is in agreement with prior results in the conditional BaxKO (Sahay et al., 2011) as well as the observation that perforant path synapse density is unaltered in germline BaxKO mice which exhibit dramatically enhanced numbers of dentate GCs (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current data combined with citations to prior studies.

claim: Synaptic integration of newborn GCs involves a redistribution of existing synapses from old to new cells.
source: Together these results support the idea that synaptic integration of newborn GCs involves a redistribution of existing synapses from old to new cells (Tashiro et al., 2006; Toni et al., 2007; McAvoy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citations to prior studies.

claim: Bax deletion promotes the synaptic integration of new GCs.
source: These results confirm that BaxKO immature GCs acquired synapses during integration and, in fact, suggest Bax deletion promotes the synaptic integration of new GCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing enhanced EPSCs in BaxKO immature GCs.

claim: The Bax/caspase signaling cascade has non-apoptotic functions in synaptic plasticity.
source: Our results show that Bax deletion increases excitatory synaptic integration of adult born GCs, consistent with growing evidence that the Bax/caspase signaling cascade has non-apoptotic functions in synaptic plasticity (Unsain and Barker, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citation to a review article.

claim: Bax activation is an intermediary step between NMDAR-Ca2+ influx and local activation of caspase-3, which is necessary and sufficient for LTD and subsequent spine pruning.
source: Prior work suggests that Bax activation is an intermediary step between NMDAR-Ca2+ influx and local activation of caspase-3, which in turn is necessary and sufficient for LTD and subsequent spine pruning (Li et al., 2010; Jiao and Li, 2011; Ertürk et al., 2014; Sheng and Ertürk, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on the molecular mechanisms of LTD and spine pruning.

claim: Loss of Bax in GCs generates a persistent enhancement of synaptic transmission consistent with a deficit in synaptic pruning.
source: Together these results show that loss of Bax in GCs generates a persistent enhancement of synaptic transmission consistent with a deficit in synaptic pruning.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing increased EPSCs and spine density in BaxKO GCs.

claim: Neurogenesis-induced loss of synapses from mature GCs requires intact Bax signaling to allow synaptic pruning.
source: Based on the above results, we predicted that neurogenesis-induced loss of synapses from mature GCs might require intact Bax signaling to allow synaptic pruning.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation/hypothesis derived from the experimental results.

claim: Neurogenesis-induced suppression of synaptic transmission to mature GCs was absent in BaxKOmat mice.
source: However, neurogenesis-induced suppression of synaptic transmission to mature GCs was absent, since the evoked EPSC was similar to controls across all stimulus intensities and the average EPSC/FV ratio was unchanged (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 7B.

claim: Neurogenesis-induced loss of synaptic strength to mature GCs requires intact Bax signaling.
source: Together, these results suggest that neurogenesis-induced loss of synaptic strength to mature GCs requires intact Bax signaling.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in BaxKOmat mice.

claim: Mature GCs exhibit experience-dependent synaptic enhancement.
source: These results show that mature GCs exhibit experience-dependent synaptic enhancement that argues against the recently described restricted period for experience-dependent plasticity of dentate GCs (Bergami et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the EE experimental data, with citation to a prior study.

claim: Increased connectivity of mature neurons after EE is likely a parallel phenomenon independent of neurogenesis.
source: Increased connectivity of mature neurons is likely a parallel phenomenon independent of neurogenesis, since similar increases in synaptic transmission and spine density occur in non-neurogenic regions (Rampon et al., 2000; Malik and Chattarji, 2012; Jung and Herms, 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citations to prior studies in non-neurogenic regions.

claim: The magnitude of increased connectivity of mature GCs after EE could be reduced by neurogenesis-induced synaptic redistribution.
source: Thus, the magnitude of increased connectivity of mature GCs could be reduced by neurogenesis-induced synaptic redistribution.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the combined results.

claim: Mature GCs undergo changes in synaptic connectivity in response to both genetic and experiential circuit manipulations.
source: Altogether, these results highlight the capacity of mature GCs to undergo changes in synaptic connectivity in response to both genetic and experiential circuit manipulations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data from genetic and EE manipulations.

claim: Selectively manipulating adult-born neurons inversely correlated with synaptic strength of mature neurons with no detectable changes in global measures of synaptic transmission.
source: We found that selectively manipulating adult-born neurons inversely correlated with synaptic strength of mature neurons with no detectable changes in global measures of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: Appropriation of existing synaptic terminals would cause mature GCs to lose synapses while the total number of synapses in the network remains constant.
source: In contrast, appropriation of existing synaptic terminals would cause mature GCs to lose synapses while the total number of synapses in the network remains constant (Figure 9C2).
evidence: This is a theoretical model presented to explain the experimental observations.

claim: The results support the model wherein newborn GCs appropriate existing synapses and consequently modify synaptic input to mature GCs.
source: By comparing measures of total synapses (fEPSPs) and synapses per mature GC (EPSCs) after selectively altering neurogenesis, our results support the latter model wherein newborn GCs appropriate existing synapses and consequently modify synaptic input to mature GCs.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: Increasing neurogenesis decreased synaptic transmission and spine density of mature GCs, consistent with the idea that immature neuron synaptic integration is a competitive process.
source: Our results showing that increasing neurogenesis decreased synaptic transmission and spine density of mature GCs is consistent with the idea that immature neuron synaptic integration is a competitive process (Tashiro et al., 2006; Toni and Sultan, 2011; McAvoy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citations to prior studies.

claim: Neurogenesis modifies synaptic transmission to existing mature GCs through a mechanism that involves reduced number of functional synapses.
source: Nevertheless, our results unambiguously demonstrate that neurogenesis modifies synaptic transmission to existing mature GCs through a mechanism that involves reduced number of functional synapses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: The results cannot be attributed to differential recruitment of local inhibitory circuits by immature GCs because GABAA receptor antagonists were used.
source: Unlike prior reports of alterations in DG excitability following selective manipulations of neurogenesis, we isolated excitatory synaptic transmission using GABAA receptor antagonists, thus our results cannot be attributed to differential recruitment of local inhibitory circuits by immature GCs (Singer et al., 2011; Massa et al., 2011; Ikrar et al., 2013; Temprana et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental design combined with citations to prior studies.

claim: Regulation of the density of mature GC excitatory synapses could potentially contribute to the finding that the number of immature GCs is inversely related to the excitability of the mature network.
source: In addition to such feedback inhibition, regulation of the density of mature GC excitatory synapses could potentially contribute to the counter-intuitive finding that the number of immature GCs is inversely related to the excitability of the mature network (Ikrar et al., 2013; Drew et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the current results combined with citations to prior studies.

claim: Differences in EPSCs cannot result from systematic differences in the number of stimulated axons because EPSCs were normalized to the simultaneously recorded fiber volley.
source: First, to account for differences in the number of stimulated axons across slices, we normalized EPSCs in mature GCs to the simultaneously recorded fiber volley, a common approach used in synaptic plasticity studies. Thus, differences in EPSCs cannot result from systematic differences in the number of stimulated axons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental methodology.

claim: Reduced evoked EPSCs were accompanied by reduced frequency of sEPSCs with no change in amplitude and no change in the PPR, which are widely accepted indicators of changes in synapse number.
source: Second, reduced evoked EPSCs were accompanied by reduced frequency of sEPSCs with no change in amplitude and no change in the PPR. These characteristics are widely accepted indicators of changes in synapse number.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Newly generated GCs usurp pre-existing synapses from mature GCs, perhaps through an activity-dependent competitive process.
source: Our results are consistent with a model wherein newly generated GCs usurp pre-existing synapses from mature GCs, perhaps through an activity-dependent competitive process (Tashiro et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citation to a prior study.

claim: Conditional suppression of spines on mature GCs enhances the integration of newborn GCs.
source: The recent observation that conditional suppression of spines on mature GCs enhances the integration of newborn GCs further supports the interactions between new and existing neurons (McAvoy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: The fEPSP does not change despite the loss of EPSCs in mature GCs due to the additional contribution of synapses on immature neurons.
source: We used fEPSPs as a primary measure of total synapses, and presumably the fEPSP does not change despite the loss of EPSCs in mature GCs due to the additional contribution of synapses on immature neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The higher intrinsic excitability of immature neurons would enable a greater contribution to fEPSPs compared to mature GCs for a given number of active AMPAR-containing synapses.
source: We did not detect any differences in the intrinsic excitability of mature GCs in our genetic models, but it is expected that the higher intrinsic excitability of immature neurons would enable a greater contribution to fEPSPs compared to mature GCs (for a given number of active AMPAR-containing synapses).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from established knowledge about immature neuron properties.

claim: Newborn GCs have a high fraction of silent synapses that may limit their contribution to fEPSPs.
source: However, newborn GCs have a high fraction of silent synapses that may limit their contribution to fEPSPs (Chancey et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Mature GCs exhibit a non-cell autonomous effect of Bax deletion from adult-born GCs (decreased EPSCs) that is opposite to the cell-autonomous effect of Bax deletion in both cell types (increased EPSCs).
source: We show that mature GCs exhibit a non-cell autonomous effect of Bax deletion from adult-born GCs (Figures 1–3, decreased EPSCs) that is opposite to the cell-autonomous effect of Bax deletion in both cell types (Figures 5–6, increased EPSCs).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: The cell autonomous function of Bax is required for the non-cell autonomous effect of Bax deletion.
source: Remarkably, the cell autonomous function is required for the non-cell autonomous effect (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: The non-cell autonomous effect of Bax deletion results from enhanced neurogenesis.
source: We propose that the non-cell autonomous effect results from enhanced neurogenesis (supported by the observation that ablation of neurogenesis produced the opposite outcome, Figure 4)
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined experimental data.

claim: The cell autonomous effect of Bax deletion results from a contribution of the Bax pathway in synaptic depression and spine pruning.
source: whereas the cell autonomous effect results from a contribution of the Bax pathway in synaptic depression and spine pruning.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with knowledge of Bax function.

claim: Caspases mediate dendritic remodeling during neural development.
source: Caspases mediate dendritic remodeling during neural development (Kuo et al., 2006b; Williams et al., 2006; Riccomagno and Kolodkin, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Caspase-3 activation is necessary and sufficient for NMDAR-mediated AMPA receptor internalization and LTD at hippocampal synapses.
source: and more recent work shows that caspase-3 activation is necessary and sufficient for NMDAR-mediated AMPA receptor internalization and LTD at hippocampal synapses (Li et al., 2010; Jiao and Li, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: LTD is associated with spine shrinkage and is typically considered a herald of synapse pruning.
source: LTD is associated with spine shrinkage and is typically considered a herald of synapse pruning (Oh et al., 2013; Wiegert and Oertner, 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Local induction of caspase-3 activity in dendrites triggers spine elimination.
source: Indeed, local induction of caspase-3 activity in dendrites triggers spine elimination whereas caspase-3 KO mice exhibit increased GC spine density (Ertürk et al., 2014; Lo et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Bax deletion enhanced synaptic strength and spine density while blocking neurogenesis-induced loss of mature GC synaptic strength, consistent with the idea that on-going synaptic refinement controls the strength of excitatory transmission.
source: Our findings that Bax deletion enhanced synaptic strength and spine density while blocking neurogenesis-induced loss of mature GC synaptic strength are consistent with the idea that on-going synaptic refinement controls the strength of excitatory transmission and that continual neurogenesis promotes a competitive environment for redistribution of synapses (McAvoy et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data combined with citation to a prior study.

claim: Both enhancing neurogenesis and blocking output from mature GCs improves performance on the same context discrimination task, suggesting that neurogenesis could contribute to DG function by modifying mature GC activity.
source: First, both enhancing neurogenesis and blocking output from mature GCs improves performance on the same context discrimination task (Sahay et al., 2011; Nakashiba et al., 2012), suggesting that neurogenesis could contribute to DG function by modifying mature GC activity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited behavioral studies.

claim: Re-distribution of active terminals away from mature GCs could transiently sparsify population activity if new GCs initially have insufficient excitatory connectivity to allow recruitment.
source: Synaptic depression and subsequent pruning are activity-dependent processes that typically require NMDA receptor activation (Shipton and Paulsen, 2014). Hence, re-distribution of active terminals away from mature GCs could transiently sparsify population activity, if new GCs initially have insufficient excitatory connectivity to allow recruitment (Dieni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results combined with citations to prior work.

claim: Enhancing neurogenesis by blocking the apoptotic pathway likely promotes competition to a greater extent than other methods of increasing neurogenesis.
source: Second, since eliminating Bax in progenitors leads to greater innervation as well as greater survival of neural progeny, enhancing neurogenesis by blocking the apoptotic pathway likely promotes competition to a greater extent than other methods of increasing neurogenesis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental results.
